Spherical convolution and support control

Reconstructed and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Earlier edition and retained figure: GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Original exposition: CC0. The supplied programme foundations retain their stated licences.

A surface measure can acquire a volume density after convolution with another surface measure. For two spheres in three dimensions, the density occupies precisely the radii between their difference and their sum. We compute its Newton potential, take its entire distributional Laplacian, and then track what happens to the center and boundary spheres under differentiation and a third convolution.

We use complex bilinear distribution pairings. Ordinary surface measure on the radius- sphere is denoted by . The elementary integration results used below, including absolute Fubini, dominated convergence, linear changes of variables and planar polar integration, are proved in the integration foundation, §§15.1, 15.6 and 16. Scalar calculus, integration by parts and the trigonometric parametrization are proved in the metric and calculus foundation, §§13.1–13.5 and 13.9. Solution 9 proves its higher Taylor formula locally.

The exact earlier distributional proofs are U021, B0–B3 and Theorems 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 (pairing, convolution, derivatives and proper support addition); U011, the graph surface construction, Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 2.2 (flux and Green identities); U020, Theorem 1.1 (the point source); and U023, the surface facts preceding Lemma 2.1 and that lemma's complete shell proof. Polar integration in three dimensions is proved in the angular foundation, A4. No external citation replaces any of these proofs.

Two surfaces produce a volume density

Theorem 1.1 (density, support and source potential). Suppose , and write Then Its support is the closed annulus , interpreted as the closed ball when . The Laplacian has no additional surface or point terms. The mass is .

Proof: latitude and area. The unit sphere has coordinates Their tangent vectors have scalar product zero and squared lengths Thus the square root of their Gram determinant is one. We justify directly that the actual graph surface measure has this density. On each open hemisphere write the surface as the graph . U011's graph density is . Planar polar integration in , with radius , gives density ; the one-dimensional substitution gives . In particular a coordinate rectangle with bounded away from and in an interior interval has area equal to the product of its two interval lengths. This calculation uses only the fundamental theorem on a compact interval. The generating-class uniqueness proof in the integration foundation, §16.2, extends equality from these rectangles to their Borel sets. Exhaustion extends it to each open hemisphere. Thus the density is for all nonnegative Borel integrands there.

The omitted equator and meridian have zero area. Away from the poles, cover each by finitely many rotated graph charts in which the curve lies on a coordinate line in the base; the graph density is bounded on a smaller chart, and that line has planar measure zero by Fubini. The poles have zero area by the cap estimate preceding U023 Lemma 2.1. Exhausting the open coordinate intervals therefore gives, first for nonnegative Borel functions and then for absolutely integrable ones, In particular the area is . Scaling each graph coordinate by multiplies its area by , so has mass . Orthogonal invariance is proved just before U023 Lemma 2.1: apply the linear change of variables to a spherical annulus and cancel its radial factor. Consequently an arbitrary unit vector may be used as the latitude axis.

Proof: computing the potential. The complete shell lemma, including a sphere through the pole, gives It is a bounded continuous function. Its convolution with the finite measure is continuous: for in a fixed compact set, uniform continuity of on the relevant compact difference set controls the translated integral uniformly. Both surface measures are compact. If their two coordinates and the sum of all three coordinates stay bounded, the third coordinate stays bounded too; closedness then makes the triple preimage compact. U021 Theorem 3.1 therefore applies to , and derivative transfer gives This is why the potential calculation identifies the original convolution.

It also follows by ordinary improper limits. Its original integrand is bounded by , so no pole remains.

Proof: all boundary terms. For , differentiating gives The product and chain rules consequently give . On the middle region, the other open regions have zero Laplacian. At , the middle value is and its derivative is zero. At , its value and derivative are and . They match the adjacent pieces.

For a compact smooth test , apply Green's identity on these regions inside a large ball outside the support of . The boundary expression is . Opposite normals at a shared sphere, together with matching values and derivatives, cancel both terms. When , the inner piece is constant and smooth through zero. When , excise the ball of radius . The value and gradient size of are bounded there; hence the two extra terms together have absolute value at most which tends to zero. Also is locally integrable, since its volume integral near zero is . Thus the limit of the bulk integrals is precisely ; there is no omitted source.

Proof: exact supports and mass. The density is strictly positive on its open annulus. Every ball meeting its closure contains an open subball where the density is positive, so a nonnegative test there has positive pairing. The distribution vanishes off that closure. This proves its exact support.

On either side of a positive boundary radius, the density is smooth, but its limiting values are zero and . A smooth representative would coincide pointwise on each open side: their smooth difference has zero distribution, and testing a neighborhood on which its real or imaginary part has fixed sign forces that difference to vanish. The distinct limits exclude such a representative at every boundary point. If , the density also exceeds every bound on an open punctured ball sufficiently near zero. A continuous representative bounded on a smaller closed ball cannot equal it on that punctured ball. Elsewhere the displayed density is smooth. This proves exactly the singular sets stated above.

Finally polar integration gives using . This is the product of the two surface areas.

If a radius is zero, its ordinary two-dimensional surface measure is the zero measure, not a unit point mass: the singleton has zero surface area. Its convolution, support and singular support are therefore zero, empty and empty. Probability surface measures below are defined only for positive radii; their limit at zero is a different assertion.

Parentheses require control of the original supports

Proposition 2.1 (existence of both expressions does not imply equality). On the real line, take the constant distribution , the locally integrable function , and the compact distribution . Then every binary convolution in exists under proper support addition.

Proof. Testing the weak derivative gives The fundamental theorem applies since vanishes past a finite point. Thus . U021's compact-factor derivative identity and point-mass identity give Both inner operations have a compact factor. Their results, zero and a point mass, are themselves compact; consequently each outer operation exists, and has the displayed value. A test with nonzero integral distinguishes them.

The original three supports are . The triples , , have sum zero and unbounded coordinates. Hence the inverse image of the compact set under their sum map is not compact. The associativity hypothesis in U021 Theorem 3.1 fails. Cancellation in the first inner convolution gives empty support and allows its next operation; it does not change the original three-support sum map.

In Theorem 1.1, two original compact factors supplied the required bound on every triple coordinate. A single compact middle factor, as in this proposition, supplies no such bound on the other two coordinates.

Exercise 2 (basic). Give the complete Newton potential of , its forcing density, support and singular support. Evaluate it at zero and at radius three. Check the values and derivatives at both interfaces.

Exercise 3 (intermediate). Let and . Convolve with . Find its density, mass and both supports, and prove the translation rule used.

Exercise 9 (advanced). Prove and expand through order . Supply all second and fourth spherical moments and an explicit sixth-order test-seminorm bound for the remainder.

Exercise 10 (advanced). Find a continuous volume density for , including its value at zero. Prove its exact singular support and highest global classical differentiability class, and integrate its mass.

Solution 10. The density of two factors is , with arbitrary finite choices at its null-set boundaries. All three measures have compact support, so their association is allowed. For , averaging this nonnegative function on the sphere gives Perform the substitution first on truncated intervals avoiding a zero denominator, then take the monotone limit. Its Jacobian cancels ; the final finite integral proves integrability even at the possible pole. Tonelli applied to a compactly supported test's absolute value identifies this pointwise integral almost everywhere with the distributional convolution. At zero direct averaging on gives .

Separating , and produces the continuous representative The values agree at both interfaces. On the middle interval its derivative is ; on the other two regions it is zero. At radius one the one-sided derivatives are and , and at radius three they are and . Restriction to a radial line through any point of either sphere rules out regularity there. A smooth distributional representative would agree on both adjacent open regions and could not remove that derivative mismatch. There are no other singularities: the function is smooth on each of those regions and constant near zero. Its exact singular support is the two spheres, and its highest global classical class is , not . In fact it is globally Lipschitz, since its radial profile has bounded slopes and .

Its total mass is The third average has removed the origin singularity and the density jumps, while the two derivative jumps remain.
